CHURCH RATES IN CIIESIIIRE. Tax Trustees of the River Weaver have at hat shown some symptoms of repentance for their late reckless extravagance with the money of Cheshire ratepayers. We under- stand that at a late meeting of the Trueteee they dismissed their Engineer or at least put such pressure on him as caused him to re- sign his office, and purpose to select from the many who are sure to offer themselves for the vacant place, one who will proceed rather slowly and surely, than try rash ex- periments at the cost of the over- burdened taxpayers. We will not de- lay to °onside: whether at the same time it would not have been wise to make a more thorough change in the staff, and to replace somewhat old and unaccom- modating officials with men better acquainted with the wants of the trade, and more ready to adopt reasonable innovations, nor was one curious to inquire whether if the unfor- tunate Engineer had been a member of the Church of England, well proved in ortho- doxy, of pleasant social habits and a genial disposition, Metered of being a member of I • small and eennewhatl austere sect, his alleged sine of extravagance and insubordin- ation might have been overlooked. But our business to-day is with another matter. As far as money has hitherto been spent the sin of the Trustees has been against the whole County, with no distinction of sect or creed. If the whole sum allowed to be borrowed by their late acts for the im- provement of the complete navigation from Winaford to Weston Point has been or is to be expended in doing the works from Wes- ton Point toNorthwich, if a lift has been con- structed where practically there are no good. to be transhipped, and the tolls will hardly pay for the oil and fuel consumed, if lecke, unnecessarily large and wasteful of water and power, have been made, if a dredge, which will not swine, has been built and has sunk, if the interests of the salt manufac- turers at the principal seat of the trade have been postponed to a distant period, and if in consequence of all theee blunder there can be no surplus revenue for County purposes for some years, at all events there has been this &knees, that the Churchmen and the Nonconformists have suffered alike. No one, except it may be a few contractore, have had any unfair advantages. But the proposal to which we called the attention of our readers a fortnight ago stands on another footing. It is a deliberate attempt to spend public money for sectarian purposes, it is a depriva- tion of all ratepayers of every denomination for the benefit of &particular sect, it is against public policy as raising a general act by a private Act of Parliament, it is opposed to common honesty and morality—as taking money given to all and epending it to the ad- vantage of a few. The only argument, if such au assertion deserves the name of argument, for the mai- practice is, that the church wee built under the provisions of an Act of Parliament, that it is tumbling down, and therefore should be rebuilt, eo that the congregation may be no worse off than they were before. Adopt this argument, and carry it out to its full extent, and there is not a single par eh church in Englaed which might not be re- built out of a rate. They exist, in the majority of ewes they have been built and restored by a church rate, and should they fall into decay, the congregation, would have an equal claim with that of the Wineford Church to their restoration out of the rates. But the wisdom of Parliament has decided that this should not be, and that the repair and restoration of our pariah churches shell be done by private contributions. What difference can there then be between a parish church built under a private Aot of Parlia- ment ? In each case the power has been exhausted, and it is unfair to renew the power in one case when it is impoeeible to renew it in the other. Such being the general rule, we do not see why the ioverty of the intended congregation makes any difference. We say " intended " because we do not, as a rule, believe that the elms of workmen for whom thew churches were built have very largely taken advantage of them. Ae a fact, they have been used by a clam somewhat, and in some instances very much, higher in the social male than the boatmen and saltboilers; and the average income of the worshippers would contrast not unfavourably with that of any of our town congregations. There are Non- conformist chapels at each of the three places, which have not only had to be built, but have to be maintained at the expense of Individuals who are no better off in the aggregate than than those who frequent the Weaver churches. Why, therefore, should these Nonconformists who support their own chapels be called upon to suffer from an in- crease in the county rate to benefit others who do not support their Church at all? The matter is so plain to all unprejudiced minds that we do not carets argue it. The facts are so clear that to state them is suffi. cient. It is a miserable outcome of an at- tempt made forty years ago to evangelize a district. If sufficient earnestneas has not been established by this time among a congrega- tions, to induce them to make sacrifices to support the fabrics of the Church in which they worship, it is a fresh proof, were any needed, that a State Church has little real influence over and inspiree small affection in the breaeta of those who are claimed as its members. There are Churches and Church- men at Winsford, there are Conservatives and Orangemen, there ;are large employers of labour, there are unfortunately men who for fashion's sake now profess to be Church- men, and have forgotten their old Noncom. fortuity, and yet these Churchmen, Conser- vatives, Orangemen, and perverts, are con- tent to stand by and see public money spent to do a work which their former neighbours chose to have done, and are doing for them- selves whenever the necessity arises. There is another clause in the print of this precious Act, in which we see danger. It to proposed to amigo districts to each of these Churches, thus making each of them the centre of an ecclesiastical district. Now the original idea of the promoters of these Churches was, that they shall be chapels for the boatmen, and the parsons in the nature , of missionaries among those employedon the river, and this idea was so fax adopted by the Trustees of the River Weaver, that we believe that up to a year or two ago, their employees on certain days in the year, re- ceived their full wages on condition of going to Church. But if districts be assigned, this special intention is set at naught. The inhabitants in this area allotted to each Church, will not be simply boatmen, but others, some richer and some poorer, and the ministration to all will be paid out of the County rate. The spiritual policies will have to act not only among those for whom the aervicee were originally designed, but among a totally different class. The Church will become part of the great ecclesiastical organisation which covers the whole country and will lose the alight missionary character they have hitherto nominally had. The Jute)," of other clergymen of the Church of England will be made lighter, and that at the expase of the ratepayers of the county. If there be any left, we will not say of the opponents, but of the promoters of the original bill, we would earnestly call upon , them to oppose a charge which strikes us to I overeetting all which they desired to effect, as postponing the cffiime of the migrating I boatman in favour of the comfortable house- holder, and as tending to create a benefice on land instead of a mission chapel for water- MOD. For every reason, therefore, we trust that the better eons.) of the Trustees will prevail, and that these objectienable clauses will not be mod, Utile; be peen; they mat be

opposed, and their defeat will probably enough involve the loss of the bill. We shall regret this, for we believe that the Truetees now may be expected to do good work. They era frightened at their expen- diture, they have learnt by their mistake' how to avoid them in the future, and if they can but have time granted to repay the ex- txavaganee of the past, and to go carefully forward with more matured plane, they may yet give substantial aid to some future generation of Cheshire ratepayers.

div.head: TRADE AND FINANCE IN 1876.
div.p: TRADE AND FINANCE IN 1876.

Tie year which has just expired has been remarkable in the commercial, not leas than in the political world. We have had no monetary crash, and comparatively few . commercial failures, for the beat of ell rea- sons, that they were anticipated and pro- vided against. Acceptances have been duly met, and so long as that is the ease, it is not at all likely that any commercial disturbance IC to be feared, In a short review of the cotton trade a few months since we ventured to say that prima were exceedingly low, and that a rice might be anticipated. This has actually occurred. The price of middliag Orleans cotton in the first week of July was Bd. per lb., and last week it was °facially quoted 841 d. The tendency of mitres has been upwards during the present week, and considering that the prospects of supply are noise good as they have hitherto apparently i been, this upward tendency is not at all to be wondered. at. Within the last twelve months the average price of raw cotton has been lower than it has been for nineteen years, while the production of the American staple lies never yet reached the maximum of the year preoeding the American war. We may safely infer that considering the cajole which the cotton trade has gone through during the last dozen years it is now in a healthy state, and the wonder is, that looking at the abundance of money, prices . are not higher. The spending capacity of the operative classes appears to be in no wise diminished; and the probability is that domestic expenditure in its varied ramifica- tions has become normal. In so far, however, as regards the cotton trade, certain circum- stances, which have been overlooked, are worthy of attention. The telegraph and the Suez Canal have revolutionised the trade to the East. Merchants no longer held large stocks of goods in anticipation of native de- mands. That they may do se at some future time is possible enough, let it is quite clear that with money ranging for months put at two per cent., that old fashioned business , has gone out for the present at least. While ' we may congratulate °woollen in escaping from a commercial panic at home, we mast , not overlook the fact that in an indirect war we have felt the effects of monetary pres- sure abroad. The United State of America ' are only beginning to recover from the de- pression which prevailed there three years since, and Germany has not yet shown any desire to support the British market as it did in former times. In looking back at the pant year, we must consider the fluctuations in the silver market. The decline in the price of silver in .the early mouths of the past year really meant a loose the exporters of Mancheeter geode to the East. The price of yarn and cloth for India and China mug be taken in conjunction with the exchanges for these eountrtee. At the close of 1875 the value of bar silver was 580. per ounce. It fell until it reached 4611 on July, and sines that time it hoe after sundry fluctuations re- . covered its former level. The excitement which prevailed in the coal and iron trade • three years since, has also completely sub- , sided during the past twelve months, but recently the depression has been less ! marked. The threatening state of affairs in the East of Europe has overruled other con- siderations within the past six months, and even now the political helm is overcast. The consequence has been, that money has flowed into this country for security and in- vetment, and the rate of interest has been unprecedentedly low during the past year. During the let few weeks, however, the bullion in the Bank of England hue very materially declined, and a rise in the Bank rate appears imminent. In fact, a revival of trade is certain to increase the demand for money, and it only sequinss a restoration of confidence to bring about such a result. The long expected and frequently predicted money panic of 1878, hits not occurred, probably because it really was an- ticipated and provided against. Bankers have been unpreoedentedly prudent and cautious eince the revelations of the Collie swindle, and the recent action of certain London Banks in giving notice that they would no longer allow interest upon current account deposit., is most sig- nificant. While reviewing the commercial aspects of the past year, we must not over- look the fad that there has been a tendency on the part of the Legislature to interfere with the legitimate laws of supply and de- mand. Labour is a purchasable commodity like anything else, and artificial restrictions and stimulants are equally mischievous. Sooner or later, they are oertain to end in disaster. In looking at our prospects for 1877, we may congratulate ourselves that during the past year we have not been sow- ing the seeds of a commercial crisis, and that prices are now so moderate that we may safely look forward to twelve months of prosperity. Even should the peace of Europe be disturbed, we think that the effects of such a calamity have been mostly discounted.
